claims.text: The initial single-crystal FeNiCrMn alloy has an FCC structure and no pre-existing BCC phase.
The FeNiCrMn alloy has a low stacking-fault energy of approximately 20 mJ/m².
Yielding is initiated primarily by thermally activated dislocation nucleation at surface defects.
Stacking-fault nucleation contributes to the onset of yielding.
The onset of yielding is not primarily driven by an FCC-to-BCC transformation.
The low strain-rate sensitivity of yield strength results from high activation-energy barriers for dislocation motion in a highly distorted lattice.
Thermal fluctuations, rather than stress-assisted processes, overcome the barriers controlling dislocation motion.
Twinning-induced plasticity is a dominant deformation mode.
Martensitic transformation produces HCP rather than BCC material during deformation.
Low stacking-fault energy facilitates local FCC-to-HCP transformation through stacking-fault accumulation.
Stacking faults and deformation twins act as precursors to HCP martensite.
Free surfaces and grain boundaries are dislocation-nucleation sites relevant to the proposed mechanism.
Crystal orientation controls the critical resolved shear stress for partial-dislocation nucleation.
Crystals loaded along <111> have higher yield strengths because multiple slip-system activation barriers must be overcome.
The alloy remains FCC-stable up to 600 K under uniaxial tension.
HCP martensite forms only at high strain or under cryogenic conditions through stacking-fault accumulation.
Yield strength has minimal strain-rate dependence but strong temperature dependence between 77 K and 600 K.
HCP phase fraction increases as temperature decreases and strain increases.
BCC phase remains absent throughout tensile deformation in the stated regime.
Traditional FCC metals such as Cu and Al have higher strain-rate sensitivity because they have easier dislocation glide and lower activation barriers.

contradictions.description: The tested material is explicitly a single crystal, but grain boundaries are listed among its dislocation-nucleation sites. The parenthetical reference to polycrystalline analogs limits this inconsistency but makes that mediator inapplicable to the stated test system.

The mechanism is described as thermally activated, yet thermal activation is contrasted with 'stress-assisted mechanisms.' Thermally activated yielding under applied load normally includes stress-dependent barrier lowering, so the proposed distinction is internally unclear.
